name: Yamato Japan (Kofun and Asuka periods)
summary: The first Japanese state, led by the Yamato kings (later emperors) from the Nara basin; they built giant keyhole-shaped tombs (kofun), adopted Buddhism and Chinese writing, and introduced Chinese-style laws in the Taika reforms (645).

knownFor.label: Kofun tombs
knownFor.note: Keyhole-shaped burial mounds, such as Daisen Kofun.

knownFor.label: Hōryū-ji
knownFor.note: One of the oldest wooden buildings in the world.

location.value: Central and western Japan, centred on the Nara basin (Yamato).

terrain.value: Mountainous islands with small coastal plains and river basins.

climate.value: Temperate, with four seasons and a rainy season in summer.

population.value: Perhaps 3–5 million people by the year 700.

urbanisation.value: Palaces and capital sites in the Asuka area, and later Fujiwara-kyō (694).

disease.value: Smallpox epidemics from the 500s, and the great smallpox epidemic of 735–37.

migration.value: Craftsmen and scholars from Korea and China.

economicBase.value: Rice farming, with iron working and fishing.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade and embassies with Korea and China.

wealth.value: Elite wealth in iron, mirrors and tombs.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes in rice and labour; first coins (Fuhonsen, about 683).

inequality.value: Clans (uji) and the royal family above farmers.

governmentType.value: Kingdom ruled by the Yamato great kings, later emperors.

keyRulers.value: Empress Suiko and Prince Shōtoku; Emperor Kōtoku, who strengthened imperial power over the clans (645).

succession.value: Within the royal family, often disputed.

institutions.value: Shōtoku’s Seventeen-article constitution, built on Confucian ideas, and the Taika reforms (645).

stability.value: The Jinshin War of 672 was a succession struggle that strengthened the throne.

eliteConflict.value: The Soga supported Buddhism and the Mononobe opposed it; the Mononobe were crushed at the Battle of Shigisan (587).

armyAndTech.value: Armoured cavalry and iron weapons, influenced by Korea and China.

majorWars.value: Yamato and Baekje forces were defeated by Tang China’s navy at the Battle of Baekgang (663).

territoryChange.value: Expanded control over Kyushu and eastern Japan.

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with Baekje; after Baekje fell (660) Yamato sent envoys straight to the Chinese court.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded, though Japan adapted Chinese writing and law.

scienceEducation.value: Chinese characters, Confucian ideas and Buddhist learning arrived from Korea and China.

openness.value: Open to trade and new ideas from abroad.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and ships linked the Yamato court to Korea and the provinces.

religion.value: Worship of the kami; Buddhism from the 500s, which spread after the Soga victory of 587.

languageWriting.value: Old Japanese written with Chinese characters.

artsArchitecture.value: Keyhole-shaped kofun tombs up to 400 m long, lined with hundreds of haniwa clay figures; the 7th-century wooden buildings of Hōryū-ji.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Kofun period; Asuka period (checked 8 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Yamato rulers and the idea of divine descent.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in pit houses or raised-floor houses and ate rice and fish.

neighbours.value: Baekje, Silla, Goguryeo, Sui and Tang China.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism and Confucian ideas from China.

riseSignals.value: Large keyhole-shaped burial mounds (kofun) appear from about 250.

declineSignals.value: No decline: the state grew into the Nara state with its first permanent capital.

outcome.value: The capital moved to Nara in 710, beginning the Nara period.

overallCertainty.value: Known from chronicles, inscriptions and archaeology; dates and numbers are approximate.
